Introduction

Why distance isn’t access

A food desert is usually drawn with distance: more than a mile from a supermarket.

But a store next door doesn’t help if it’s too expensive, dirty, empty, or closed when you get off work.

Penchansky & Thomas (1981), adapted to food by Caspi et al. (2012)

AvailabilityIs the food there? · Stock, selection, empty shelves
AccessibilityCan I get there? · Distance, parking, the bus
AccommodationDoes it fit my life? · Hours, SNAP/WIC, pickup, checkout
AffordabilityCan I pay for it? · Prices, deals, value
AcceptabilityDoes it meet my standards? · Freshness, cleanliness, staff
Access has five dimensions. Distance measures one of them.

Introduction

Teresa’s idea: reviews are a survey nobody had to run

How one review becomes part of a score

  • 1

    Read the text

    Each review becomes 384 numbers (a sentence model)

  • 2

    Group similar reviews

    Reviews cluster into topics: “parking”, “prices”, “rude cashiers”

  • 3

    Name the dimension

    Each topic matches the dimension whose definition it sounds most like

  • 4

    Good or bad from the stars

    1★ = −1, 2–4★ = 0, 5★ = +1

  • 5

    Store, then neighborhood

    Average per store, pooled; nearby stores weighted into each census tract

Teresa’s pilot

49 stores

about 25,000 Google reviews, Raleigh

Her finding

Reviews work

They sort into the five dimensions, and tract scores differ by race and income

The text decides which dimension a review is about. The stars decide good or bad.

Goal

What were we trying to do?

Goal: score every grocery store and census tract in North Carolina on the five dimensions of access, using Teresa’s method.

01

Every store

A complete list of NC grocery stores, with a written rule for what counts

02

Every review

Every Google review we can reach for each store, checked against Google’s counts

03

Reproduce first

Show our data gives Teresa’s Raleigh results before changing anything

04

Then improve

Fix what testing finds, one change at a time, each measured against her method

A method that works for 49 stores has to be rebuilt to work for 4,442. Reproducing her results is what makes the rest credible.

What made the scraper trustworthy

  • 1

    Open the store by its exact Google ID

    The first version searched by name. A Sam’s Club in Hendersonville came back as one in Raleigh.

  • 2

    Check every scroll actually moved

    A scroll that silently does nothing looks exactly like the end of the list

  • 3

    One scraper per machine

    Google limits by IP address. NC State Linux machines, plus ISE 408 students early on

  • 4

    Never delete

    Suspect reviews are set aside with a reason, so any decision can be undone

A September audit found wrong-store scrapes. We fixed the code and the data before collecting the rest.

Step 7 · Pipeline B

What did testing find, and how did we fix it?

Provisional · before hand labeling
Problem found in AFix in Pipeline BResult
One topic per review, but 79% of longer reviews cover 2+ subjectsRead reviews sentence by sentenceFinds 70% of labels, not 45%
Her definitions put selection under AcceptabilityDefinitions written from the raters’ rulesAvailability recall 0.50 → 0.81
A 3★ “great selection, high prices” scores 0 on bothGood or bad read from each sentence’s text84% right (stars: 64%)
One 5★ review can top a rankingBetter pooling: count model, county and store-type levelsHalf the error for stores with ≤5 reviews
exp(−miles) is an urban ruleReal drive times on OpenStreetMap roads, 16-minute marketsShows who has no store in reach
Each fix is one switch, scored against Teresa’s method on the same yardsticks.

Hand labeling

What only people can do

  • 1

    Label reviews

    260 reviews, 5 people each. For each dimension: not discussed, positive, negative or mixed. This is the answer key.

  • 2

    Check topics

    83 topics in about 25 groups. Mark vague ones, score each group 0–3 per dimension. This decides which reviews count.

  • 3

    Import and rerun

    One script imports the labels, takes the majority vote and reruns everything: about 1.5 hours.

The biggest single call

Topic 0

58,000 reviews about “the grocery store”. Generic label, but much of it is about selection: Availability’s best evidence.

Tested

Nov 15

The whole after-labeling path ran end to end on fake labels from five raters

Until people label, every score is provisional. After, one command produces the final numbers.

Results · Dimensions

Are there really five dimensions?

Provisional · before hand labeling

How stores perform

2 dimensions

Overall quality (clean, staffed, stocked) and price. A store that does well on one access topic does well on nearly all of them, except price.

What people talk about

14–15 themes

Mostly product mix. The strongest theme the five A’s don’t name: checkout (self-checkout, registers, lines). Then refunds and service, and the trip itself (parking, pickup, crowds).

Method: group topics by how they rise and fall together across 1,803 stores, the way the Big Five personality traits were found. Keep only factors that return in 50 bootstrap samples.

For scores, the five carry about two independent pieces of information. Checkout is the leading candidate for a sixth.

Limits

What’s wrong with the data?

01

Answer key is a stand-in

Accuracy numbers measure agreement with Claude until people label

02

Some stores don’t belong

3 have addresses outside NC; 37 are listed by Google as restaurants

03

Small samples

Median store: 5 reviews on Accommodation, 7 on Accessibility

04

Big stores hold newest reviews only

257 stores, a quarter of all reviews

05

Dates are vague

“3 years ago” · good to about a year

06

State lines

Only NC stores: border tracts look worse than they are

Every limit is written down, and most are flagged in the files, so a study can filter or adjust for it.

Lessons

What got in the way, and what did I learn?

ChallengeWhat it meantLesson
The first store list came from one sourceIt would have drawn food deserts that were holes in the listThe frame decides everything downstream. Check coverage before collecting
The scraper trusted namesWrong-store reviews got into the dataVerify by identity, not by name
Scrapes that “finished” earlySilent failures look exactly like successCheck that every step actually did something
Teresa’s method is a few notebooksUnstated choices (units, tract list) had to be reverse-engineeredReplicate first, then improve, and write down every change
Everyone wants new resultsImprovements made before the baseline can’t be judgedKeep the faithful version next to the improved one
Most of the hard work was making the data trustworthy, not the modeling.

Backup · Method

The ten decision tests

TestQuestionAnswer
D1Which definition text did Teresa use?First-person: reproduces her numbers to 0.002, 9/9 of her hand-scored topics
D2Is one topic per review enough?Rankings mostly survive (ρ ≥ 0.85); sentences find a third more labels → B
D344, 83 or 168 topics?Results barely move (F1 0.59–0.60). Keep 83
D4Reassign outlier reviews to a topic?Yes: triples coverage, ranks barely change
D5Merge near-duplicate topics for the hand check?Yes: halves the work, 20 of 23 groups agree
D6Frozen Raleigh model or NC refit?Report both: frozen for Raleigh, refit for NC stores
D7Translate non-English reviews?No: 99.5% of 8+ word reviews are English
D8Does the replication hold after pooling?Yes: ρ 0.90–0.95
D9Her Table 5.3 units and tracts?Share and $10k; tract list unknown
D10Where do definitions sit among the topics?Availability’s nearest reviews are in Topic 0

Backup · Pooling

Why A’s top stores have one or two reviews

Provisional · before hand labeling

Median reviews behind each method’s top-10 stores

A store whose reviews on a dimension are all 5★ has a standard error of zero. Teresa’s code floors it at one in a million, so the model treats the store as perfectly measured and doesn’t shrink it.

B5 models the counts of low, neutral and high reviews and adds county and store-type levels. On held-out reviews it halves A’s error for stores with five or fewer reviews.

A keeps the floor because it’s Teresa’s method. B fixes it.

Backup · Sentiment

Why read good or bad from the text?

Provisional · before hand labeling

Gold-set polarity, all 424 labeled pairs

84% vs 64%

text vs stars. Stars call 33% of these “neutral”.

Reviews with 2–4 stars (138 pairs)

66% vs 0%

Stars can’t say anything about a middle review. The text gets two-thirds right.

The sentiment reader is a logistic regression on the review vectors, trained on 400,000 reviews. 74% accurate on 100,000 held-out reviews; its score correlates 0.80 with stars. Store scores from text and from stars rank stores alike (ρ 0.82–0.94).

Backup · Scraper

Scraper engineering: what turned out to be hard

LessonWhat happened
Verify by identityName search sent the scraper to the wrong store. It now opens each store by Google ID and rejects a page whose ID differs.
A silent scroll looks like the endThe scraper picked the wrong panel and declared stores complete after one screen. Every scroll now checks it moved.
Resumability is everythingState lives in SQLite. An interrupted store restarts cleanly. Counts are re-read from disk, never kept in memory.
Two kinds of blockA sign-in wall burns the account: rotate logins. A CAPTCHA burns the IP: pause 30–60 minutes.
Retry before you give up190 stores looked capped by Google. One more pass on a fresh session returned 24,481 more reviews.

Backup · Glossary

Terms used in this deck

TermMeaning
TopicA cluster of reviews about the same thing, found by the model
PoolingPulling small-sample store scores toward the average, more for stores with fewer reviews
ρ (rho)Spearman rank correlation: 1 = same order, 0 = unrelated
Recall / F1Share of true labels found / balance of finding them and being right
Census tractA Census area of about 4,000 people; NC has 2,672 with data
Frozen armTeresa’s saved Raleigh model, applied unchanged to NC reviews
Gold setThe 260 reviews people label: the answer key
